It includes identifying relevant past work, extracting claims and evidence, adapting language to new funder requirements, and maintaining continuity. It sits within grant proposal development, not peer review or project execution. The site's library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims can serve as source material for such drafting.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on document repositories, citation databases, and text processing tools that index past proposals, papers, and reports. A working setup may include a shared drive of prior submissions, a reference manager, and a searchable corpus of extracted claims. The site's catalogue of 91 AI books, 801 scientific models, and 732 AI tools provides background material, but the core infrastructure is the researcher's own archive of past work. No special hardware is required beyond standard office computing.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The practitioner first searches past work for relevant objectives, methods, results, and claims, then maps those to the new call's evaluation criteria. They extract reusable sentences and data points, rephrase them to fit the new funder's language, and check that every claim is supported by the original source. The site's 674 glossary terms can help align terminology across fields. The process is iterative: draft, compare against past evidence, and revise for consistency.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Reusing past work raises questions of authorship, data ownership, and funder-specific rules about prior disclosure. The drafter must track which text, figures, and claims came from which original paper or proposal, and confirm that reuse is permitted under any grant conditions or institutional policies. The site links to original papers rather than a search tool, which supports provenance checking. Risks include self-plagiarism, misrepresenting old results as new, and breaching confidentiality of unfunded proposals.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting from past work is moving toward more structured reuse, with claim extraction and versioned proposal libraries becoming standard practice. As research groups accumulate larger archives, tools that match past claims to new funding calls will reduce manual searching. The site's extracted claims and model catalogue point toward a future where a drafter can assemble a proposal skeleton from verified prior work, then focus effort on the novel parts. The main constraint will remain human judgment about fit and honesty.
